stories.title: Figure's F.03 humanoid passes nine straight days on a treadmill: 348 miles and 1.2 million steps
paragraphs: Figure's Brett Adcock posted on Oct. 19 that the company's F.03 humanoid robot had just crossed nine straight days walking on a treadmill, covering 348 miles and 1.2 million steps. The post includes a video.
Adcock wrote that the run started as a side project to stress the robot and expose any failures, and that the team wants to see how long it can keep going. He did not give an end date for the test.

stories.title: Agility's co-founder says Digit 5 trades running for real work: 23-kilogram lifts, a 9-minute recharge and human-style legs
paragraphs: Agility Robotics co-founder Jonathan Hurst writes in an IEEE Spectrum essay published Oct. 19 that the company has just launched Digit 5, which he says is designed to be the first humanoid robot that can safely and economically do useful work at scale. According to Hurst, Digit 5 is engineered to lift 23-kilogram bins onto high shelves and to handle heavy warehouse tasks shift after shift.

Agility announced on Oct. 15 that battery maker Nyobolt is supplying Digit 5's fast-charging battery system, which the company says gives about 90 minutes of runtime and recharges in about 9 minutes, a 10-to-1 ratio of work to charging time compared with 2-to-1 for Digit 4. Agility says that should let one robot work more than 20 hours in a 24-hour day. Hurst writes that the charging dock will deliver 240 amperes at 48 volts, and that the battery and its cooling system take up about 75 percent of the robot's torso.

Hurst writes that all the extra bulk means Digit 5 can no longer run or jump the way earlier Digits could, and that in some ways it "feels more like a forklift than the graceful humanoid I set out to build." He says humanlike legs replace the ostrichlike legs of earlier versions because the backward-knee design made the ankle strike the ground when squatting to lift objects near the floor. Agility says that when Digit 5 detects an approaching person, it lowers itself to the floor and cuts power to its motors, which the company believes is the only near-term approach to verifiably reduce risk when working near people.

Hurst calls Digit 5 the largest, heaviest and most expensive robot Agility will ever build. According to the essay, Agility's RoboFab factory in Salem, Oregon, a 70,000-square-foot facility, has the capacity to produce more than 10,000 Digit 5 robots per year, and the company's road map goes beyond carrying bins to picking individual items, tending machines, preparing parts for assembly and shipping, and eventually assembly work itself.

stories.title: Agility moves closer to becoming a publicly traded humanoid company
paragraphs: Agility Robotics says the SEC declared its registration statement with Churchill Capital Corp XI effective on Oct. 13, a key step in its planned merger with the Nasdaq-listed company. Churchill XI shareholders are set to vote on the deal on Nov. 2, and Agility expects to trade under the ticker AGLT once it closes.

Agility says its earlier Digit robots have logged more than 65,000 hours of real-world work, with deployments and agreements at companies including Schaeffler, GXO and Toyota Motor Manufacturing Canada. On Oct. 19 it added that former UPS president Mark Vale is expected to join its board as audit committee chair after the merger closes.

stories.title: China's humanoid makers: AGIBOT teases new robots for Oct. 29, Unitree adds swarm control
paragraphs: Shanghai-based AGIBOT says it will unveil new robots and new AI models at its Innovation Day on Oct. 29 at the Shanghai World Expo Center. The company has not shared details yet; earlier this month it showed its A3 Ultra, X2, OmniHand and D1 EDU platforms to researchers at the IROS 2026 conference.

Unitree, meanwhile, introduced UniUni, a system for controlling groups of its robots at once. Unitree says it can quickly choreograph swarm movements and formations, monitor each machine's status in real time and apply safety braking. In September the company also released a 22-joint robotic hand, the Dex5-S, starting at $6,500, and open-sourced its UnifoLM-WLA-1.0 robot foundation model.

stories.title: Eka Robotics raises $150 million at a $1.45 billion valuation for a robot-grasping model built on force, not just vision
paragraphs: Eka Robotics, a startup founded by MIT professor Pulkit Agrawal and former Google DeepMind researcher Tuomas Haarnoja, has closed a $150 million Series A round that values it at $1.45 billion post-money, TechCrunch reported on Oct. 20. According to TechCrunch, the round was led by the venture funds a16z and F-Prime. The company builds a manipulation system that combines a force-sensitive gripper with a new kind of deep-learning model.

TechCrunch reports that Eka's robot can pick up about 1,500 objects weighing up to 1 kilogram in an hour, compared with about 600 for a human, and that Eka says it reliably picks up objects more than 95% of the time. Instead of a vision-language-action model, the company describes its approach as a vision-force-action model that focuses on force inputs. "Vision tells you roughly where the object is, what the pose is, but the actual grabbing, the actual searching is happening through forces," Agrawal told TechCrunch.

According to TechCrunch, Eka designed its own robotic hand with more force sensors than traditional grippers, and it trains the model with reinforcement learning in a physics simulator run at scale rather than relying on human demonstration videos; the founders say they can generate thousands of hours of robot experience in minutes. Kris Hauser, a professor at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, told TechCrunch the robot "was able to adapt to a large number of different objects without retraining." Raghu Raguram, the a16z general partner who co-led the round, told TechCrunch the system is already exceeding superhuman performance for certain tasks.

TechCrunch notes that Eka still has to prove itself in the field: the company is running pilots with a number of industrial customers in pick-and-place and wire handling. Agrawal told TechCrunch the gripper hardware costs less than $1,000 and is rated for 5 million duty cycles, with a goal of reaching the 20 million cycles of standard industrial arms. Hauser said a big challenge will be running on real assembly lines "without breaking for an entire year."

stories.title: Gecko Robotics gets an extra $300 million on its U.S. Navy contract for ship-inspection robots
paragraphs: Pittsburgh-based Gecko Robotics has earned an additional $300 million on its contract with the U.S. Navy and the General Services Administration, The Robot Report reported on Oct. 20. According to the report, the increase quadruples the contract's ceiling value and comes six months after an initial $71 million IDIQ (indefinite delivery, indefinite quantity) contract award. The work is aimed at cutting maintenance delays and improving fleet readiness.

Gecko says its AI and robotic technology can save the Navy up to $8 million in repair costs per ship by identifying structural issues up to 50 times faster than traditional methods, cutting inspections from months to days. Central to the expansion, according to the report, is Gecko's Komodo system, which scans through thick non-skid deck coatings without stripping or damaging them and produces a full-deck heatmap of corrosion and material thickness, so repair teams can plan work before a ship enters drydock.

The Robot Report says Gecko's wall-climbing robots, drones and fixed sensors collect data on the health of Navy ships and submarines, including hulls, decks and welds, and that AI is used to build models that identify current and future structural problems. "The conversation around AI and robotics in defense is no longer about experimental technology. It's about delivering measurable and impactful returns," said Jake Loosararian, Gecko's co-founder and CEO. The report notes that the chief of naval operations has set a target of 80% fleet readiness.
